extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners advising on examination/obviousness)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and documenting obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) determinations during patent examination, including defining the invention as a whole, level of ordinary skill, establishing a prima facie case, and acceptable rationales for finding obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosed inherent properties part of 'invention as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In delineating the invention as a whole, look not only to subject matter literally recited in the claim but also to those properties of the subject matter which are inherent in the subject matter and are disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Antonie — consider inherent parameters (tank volume to contactor area) disclosed in specification as part of invention; In re Papesch — a compound and all its properties are inseparable. However, 'Obviousness cannot be predicated on what is not known at the time an invention is made,' (In re Rijckaert). See MPEP § 2112 for inherency rejection requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety, including portions that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must be considered as a whole, including portions that would lead away from the claimed invention; teachings that discourage the claimed solution must be considered in obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: W.L. Gore v. Garlock — prior art that teaches slow stretching of PTFE teaches away from rapid stretching; such teach-away can undercut a motivation-to-combine argument. But mere disclosure of alternatives does not necessarily constitute teaching away (In re Fulton). See MPEP § 2123.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider may include: (A) type of problems encountered in the art; (B) prior art solutions to those problems; (C) rapidity with which innovations are made; (D) sophistication of the technology; (E) educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all factors will be present and one or more may predominate. The hypothetical person of ordinary skill is a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton (KSR). See cases: In re GPAC; Custom Accessories; Environmental Designs. The person should be capable of understanding pertinent principles (Ex parte Hiyamizu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of post-dating or unpublished documents to show level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: References that postdate the claimed invention or unpublished/internal materials may be relied upon to show the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Erlich; Thomas & Betts v. Litton — unpublished internal materials, though not prior art, can indicate the level of skill; Nat'l Steel Car — non‑widely disseminated documents can demonstrate a motivation to combine implicit in the knowledge of one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying a particular level of skill not necessary where prior art reflects appropriate level
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts regarding level of skill are found in the prior art of record, the court has held that an invention may be held obvious without a specific finding of a particular level when the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Chore-Time Equipment v. Cumberland; Okajima v. Bourdeau.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain level of ordinary skill to maintain objectivity and avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the level of ordinary skill is necessary to maintain objectivity so that the obviousness inquiry is made from the perspective of a hypothetical person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention, not from the inventor, judge, layman, or genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must avoid impermissible hindsight based on applicant's disclosure (KSR). See Ryko Mfg. v. Nu‑Star and Environmental Designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness framework and burden allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, the examiner must first set forth a prima facie case, supported by evidence, showing why the claims would have been obvious in light of the prior art; once set forth, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut with evidence or argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner bears the initial factual burden; absent a prima facie case the applicant need not submit secondary evidence. If a prima facie case is made, applicant may submit evidence (e.g., comparative test data). Consider compact prosecution goals; evidence submitted after final may be denied entry. See ACCO Brands v. Fellowes and cited CCPA cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's required articulation in a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (A–D)
rubrics_metrics.description: When indicating a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the examiner should set forth: (A) relevant teachings of prior art relied upon (with citations); (B) differences between the claim and applied references; (C) proposed modification(s) of the applied references necessary to arrive at the claimed subject matter; (D) explanation why the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant column/page/line where appropriate. Positive inclusion of every reference relied upon is required (In re Hoch). Clear communication of rationale helps applicants respond and supports later interpretation of issued patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must provide articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness rejections cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning linking factual findings to the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR requires the analysis supporting a rejection be made explicit; In re Kahn and Ball Aerosol emphasize that absent articulated rationale, findings that a combination is 'common sense' are insufficient. Office personnel must provide appropriate factual findings (see MPEP § 2141, § 2143).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding hindsight and stepping into shoes of person of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: To reach a proper 103 determination the examiner must step backward in time to the perspective of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill just before the invention was made and avoid reliance on applicant's disclosure as hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of applicant’s disclosure must be put aside when determining differences and conducting the search, though it may inform evaluation of the 'subject matter as a whole.' The ultimate determination is based on the entire record by a preponderance of evidence; examiner's prima facie case must be supported by facts from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A — Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported where prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference), one of ordinary skill could have combined them by known methods, each element performs its known function in combination, and the combined results are predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate findings: (1) prior art included each element; (2) one skilled could have combined elements by known methods and each element performs same function; (3) one skilled would have recognized results were predictable; (4) any additional Graham findings necessary. If any finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot be used. Examples: Anderson’s-Black Rock (combination yielded no new function); United States v. Adams (predictability requirement and teaching away).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B — Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported by a simple substitution of a known element for another where the substitution yields predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires demonstration that substitution would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill and that factual findings support the substitution rationale (link to Graham inquiries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C — Use of a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported where a known technique is applied to improve devices/methods/products that are similar, and the improvement would have been predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must explain factual basis for similarity and predictability and tie those facts to the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D — Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement yields predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported by applying a known technique to a known device (or method/product) that is ready for improvement, producing predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the device was 'ready for improvement' and that a skilled artisan would predict the results; factual findings required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E — 'Obvious to try' with finite, predictable solutions and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' can support obviousness where there is a finite number of identified, predictable solutions and a reasonable expectation of success in trying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must show predictability and reasonable expectation of success; mere conjecture or large-scale trial-and-error does not suffice. Tie factual findings to legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F — Known work in one field prompting predictable variations for same or different field
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or different field based on design incentives or market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should identify the design incentives/market forces or other reasons why the variation would be predictable; provide supporting factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G — Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported where some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art would have led one of ordinary skill to modify a reference or to combine reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teaching/suggestion/motivation can be explicit or implicit; examiners must articulate the factual basis for why the prior art would prompt the modification or combination (link to Graham findings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Any rationale must link factual findings to the legal conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rationale employed to support obviousness must provide a link between the factual findings and the legal conclusion of obviousness; appropriate Graham factual findings are required to apply enumerated rationales properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of rationales is not all-inclusive; examiners may rely on other rationales but must provide factual findings that explain why the conclusion of obviousness follows from those facts. See discussion and examples in MPEP § 2143 and cited cases (KSR, Ball Aerosol, Van Os).
